summary:
Oman is a destination trans and gender-nonconforming travellers should avoid. The Penal Law (Royal Decree 7/2018) criminalises same-sex conduct with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, and its provisions on impersonation and gender non-conformity reach presentation as well as acts. The Public Prosecution has stated that any male who appears in female clothing or demeanour may be fined up to OMR 3,000 and jailed for up to one year, with additional charges available for publishing such material on social media. These provisions are applied to foreign nationals.

The statute set is broad. Article 265 covers public indecency, punishable by 10 days to 3 months and a fine of OMR 100 to 300. Article 266 covers impersonation and entry into women-only venues while disguised, carrying 1 month to 1 year, and reaches gender non-conformity through Article 266(d). Articles 267 and 268 cover producing or sharing content held to violate public morals, offline and online, with penalties of up to one year and 10 days to one month respectively. The Cyber Crime Law 2011, Articles 17 and 31, is used against LGBT expression and carries 1 month to 3 years plus a fine of OMR 100 to 3,000.

Courts impose custody on this basis. In September 2018 the Public Prosecution reported that a Salalah preliminary court had sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and posting photographs of themselves in women's clothing on social media, and had sentenced two further men to three years with the same fine for appearing in the video. The sentences were handed down under Article 22 of the July 2018 penal code. They followed arrests by the Royal Oman Police in January 2018 of a group of men for dressing as women after photographs circulated on social media.

Enforcement against gender expression is active and recent. In an open letter of 13 July 2020 Human Rights Watch addressed arrests and convictions under the 2018 code's 'imitating the opposite sex' provision: the Royal Oman Police announced the arrest of men in women's clothing after photographs from a private party in Salalah circulated on Snapchat, and an Asian expatriate wearing an abaya and niqab was detained during a women-only hour at a park in Al Buraimi. Human Rights Watch's April 2018 regional report records that Oman's 2018 penal code, effective that year, added a provision punishing any man who 'appears to dress in women's clothing', alongside the country's existing criminalisation of same-sex conduct and barriers to LGBT organising.

Foreign nationals face removal in addition to imprisonment. Article 60 requires deportation of a foreign national convicted of a felony, permanently, and allows it after a misdemeanour conviction on a 3-to-15-year basis. Prosecution does not depend on a family complaint: cases are frequently opened on digital evidence surfaced during unrelated investigations, and Article 49's dual-criminality exception is recorded in that context. The state ISP Omantel enables surveillance, outing carries social as well as criminal risk, and the Civil Associations Law restricts assembly and advocacy.

Border treatment reaches visibly gender-nonconforming visitors. On 27 February 2023 a genderqueer, non-binary Indian model and activist arriving at Muscat International Airport on a 10-day tourist visa reported that her companions cleared immigration while she was held for separate examination, made to remove her shirt and touched inappropriately by officers. This is first-hand evidence of how a visitor who does not present in line with sex expectations is handled at the primary port of entry.

Oman bans legal gender recognition and explicitly bans gender-affirming healthcare, and recent legislative developments have deepened the criminalisation of gender expression, according to a joint stakeholder submission by Cairo 52 and White Tent filed on 6 August 2025 for Oman's fourth-cycle Universal Periodic Review. The submission states that Oman has ignored earlier review recommendations concerning gender identity, gender expression and access to health services, and recommends ending criminalisation, adopting an anti-discrimination law and permitting legal recognition.
tangentialFactors:
The 2018 code sits within a documented regional pattern rather than an isolated statute. Human Rights Watch's 2018 regional report places Oman's new cross-dressing provision alongside Kuwait's 2007 imitation law and other gender-expression offences across the Middle East and North Africa, and records barriers to LGBT organising across the region.

Digital exposure is the ordinary trigger for prosecution. Photographs and videos shared on Snapchat and other platforms preceded the January 2018 arrests and the September 2018 Salalah convictions, and prosecutions are said to arise from digital material found during unrelated investigations rather than from complaints by family members. Visitors should assume that private images are prosecutable material.

The state ISP's surveillance capacity compounds this. Omantel is the state-owned provider, so network traffic is not anonymous, and the Cyber Crime Law's online provisions reach publishing and sharing rather than publication to the public at large.

Restrictions on association narrow what support a visitor could reach: the Civil Associations Law governs assembly and advocacy, so there is no lawful advocacy infrastructure to fall back on, and no anti-discrimination law is in force.

A rights documentation group's country profile on Oman was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying profile is understood to document criminalisation of same-sex activity and gender expression, but its contents could not be checked directly in this pass.
localsOnly:
Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, and gender-affirming healthcare is explicitly banned, so medical transition cannot be pursued lawfully within Oman.

Gender non-conformity is punishable in its own right through Article 266(d) and through the July 2018 Article 22 provision on appearing in female clothing or demeanour, meaning presentation alone can ground a charge carrying up to OMR 3,000 and one year's imprisonment.

Expatriate residents face removal: Article 60 makes deportation mandatory on a felony conviction and discretionary on a misdemeanour, so a conviction ends residency as well as imposing a sentence.

Organising is constrained by the Civil Associations Law, and Oman has not adopted anti-discrimination legislation, leaving no statutory complaint route for identity-based mistreatment.

Cases have reached prison sentences in Salalah, and the Royal Oman Police have publicly announced arrests under the cross-dressing offence, indicating that enforcement is carried out and publicised rather than confined to private complaint.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile on Oman returned HTTP 403 at research time, so the profile's own findings could not be verified directly in this pass; the criminalisation claim is carried by the statute-level extraction and court reporting instead.

The reading of Article 49's dual-criminality exception in relation to prosecution practice is unresolved: the source places it alongside the statement that cases are opened without a family complaint, but does not set out how the exception operates in practice for conduct by foreign nationals.

The deportation period of 3 to 15 years attached to misdemeanour convictions in the source is stated without explaining what the period measures; it may refer to a re-entry bar rather than to timing of removal.

No sourced information was found on where people convicted of cross-dressing or same-sex conduct are housed within Oman's prison system, or on their access to healthcare, legal representation or Complaints mechanisms while detained.

Border evidence rests on a single documented incident at Muscat International Airport in February 2023; treatment at other entry points, and the screening questions used at immigration, are not sourced.

The 2025 UPR submission is an NGO stakeholder document, not a government statement; Oman's official response to the fourth-cycle recommendations is not included in this inventory.
